τέλος [end] is not infrequently joined with genitives of nouns in periphrasis.
office, power
band, order
i.e. it has been completed.
concerning death
as θανάτου τέλος [the end of death] in Homer and other poets in periphrasis for θάνατος [death]: see Thes. vol. 7 p. 1993.
Concerning the fulfillment or gratification of a vow
Concerning the dignity such as belongs to one who holds a magistracy
which the scholiast explains as ἀντὶ τοῦ τέθριππα καὶ ἑξάϊππα τάγματα [instead of four-horse and six-horse teams]; and from this it indicates the number of horses.

τέλος ἀθανάτων [the company of the immortals] seems to be said of the assembly of the gods (in Hesychius s.v. ἐναροκτάντας [slayer of men]) which Hesychius interprets: ὁ δὲ ἐναροκτάντας θάνατος [but the death of the slayer of men] (θάνατον [death] in the codex) μὴ ἐπικαυχώμενος τὸ ἐκ τῶν θεῶν τέλος ὑψοῦ ἀπολείψει τὰ τῶν ἀθανάτων ὕψη καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ἥξει [not boasting over the end from the gods, he will leave the heights of the immortals on high and will come upon his enemies].
τέλη [rites] are called mysteries or initiations: on which see Thes. vol. 7 p. 2000.

Thus I corrected for ἔφριξ ἔρως δέ [love shuddered], which Brunck wrote as ἔφριξ᾽ ἔρωτι [I shuddered with love], as Sophocles Aj. 693 said ἔφριξ᾽ ἔρωτι, περιχαρὴς δ᾽ ἀνεπτόμαν [I shuddered with love, and in great joy I was excited], and as regards τέλους [rite], OC. 1050 οὗ πότνιαι σεμνὰ τιθηνοῦνται τέλη [where the august goddesses tend the rites], which the scholiast explains by τελετάς [rites], comparing this verse of Aeschylus.
In a broader sense τέλη [rites] is said of any sacred offerings which are made to the gods, as often in Sophocles, about which I have spoken in the Lexicon Sophocleum p. 471, once in Aeschylus

i.e. to whom these rites are owed for the expiation of dreams, where Thomas Magister does not correctly explain it as οἵτινές εἰσι τῶν τοιούτων ἔφοροι [who are the overseers of such things]. For similar examples from Euripides see Thes. vol. 7 p. 1998.

Pollux 3,38 noted that τέλος [rite] is used for γάμος [marriage]: τέλος ὁ γάμος ἐκαλεῖτο [the marriage was called τέλος]. Hence Homer and others said τέλος γάμου [the consummation of marriage] of completed nuptials: see Thes. vol. 7 p. 1993.
In the same sense τέλος γαμήλιον [marriage rite] in Aeschylus
διὰ τέλους [through to the end] to the end or to the very limit: see Thes. vol. 7 p. 1997.
Adverbially τέλος [finally] at last, in frequent use, on which see Thes. vol. 7 p. 1996.

through which strife came and the end of death,
